title.narrative: Power of Pride Asia

description.narrative: 1. Individual LGBTI know and accept their SOGIESC and can ensure their rights in society are respected. They can meaningfully engage with societal structures. 2 A support system for LGBTI is developed based on discussions about common issues, needs and challenges, creating the motivation to act against discrimination and marginalisation. 3 LGBTI CBOs can strategically engage in societal and political decision-making processes using evidence-based advocacy. 4 Agile LGBTI movements are built that can work collectively to create social and political change and respond flexibly to various situations. 5 Institutions and other allies have an internal drive to include LGBTI in their decision-making and other structures. LGBTI are actively engaged in processes and all policy-making spaces. 6 Strong and reliable laws and policies are in place for LGBTI and are enforced by all relevant bodies. Follow-up on these policies and their implementation are under scrutiny
Working towards diverse and inclusive societies in which LGBTI are able to participate to their full potential

comment.narrative: Baseline was produce in collaboration with partners in country. Consultants typically had virtual meetings with members of the participatory grant making mechanism, or representatives of partners in the country. During these meetings consultants reflected together with the partners on how best to collect the baseline data and considered the different options for who could undertake the research. In some countries it was agreed that partners would directly collect the data and in other cases partners confirmed the appointment of or co-selected a researcher. Consultants contracted with relevant organisations or individuals in each country and ensured that they were briefed about the process, provided the organisations with the baseline template as well as the tools that had been developed and how best to administer them. The research in each country then took different forms including a desktop review, which included integrating data from the Country Context Analyses (CCA)and other relevant documents, facilitating focus groups (some hybrid) as well as individual interviews and surveys with each of the partners to collect qualitative data and quantitative data. Some countries also had interviews with allies. In addition, Consultants were able to administer survey to members of the LGBTI communities either directly at events or circulated via email, by partners or by the researchers. In total consultants received 162 partner responses and 1359 member responses to the surveys.
Targets were defined by baseline consultants following baseline numbers and percentages allocated per long term outcome in the years to come to calculate targets for the countries and overall program

Through the programme we have worked hard to provide information to LGBTI community members, contributing to more understanding and knowledge of individual coping strategies. In one of our country partners, for instance, partners hosted a series of community round tables to discuss empowerment, SRHR, (cyber)bullying, mental health challenges, legal awareness, and socio-economic empowerment. As a result, participants of the round tables have formed their own social networks to stay in contact via group chat. In three different countries we have contributed with the programme to improving the self-esteem and knowledge on SOGIESC of 50 LGBTI living with disabilities, 20 GBMSM and transwomen living with HIV and 20 GBMSM and 83 transgender people. In another country, a partner organisation empowered and inspired young queer women creatives with a storytelling contest that led to an online campaign for youth, bringing visibility to LGBTI narratives. Finally, despite the challenges of two of our most difficult contexts, partners decided to focus on what they could do for their communities and closed 2021 with a milestone each. In one of them, partners managed to create an online space that gathers resources, promotes awareness, and mitigates the isolation of individuals who lack a physical community. In the other one, partners decided to make psychosocial counselling available for 60 LBQT community members.

Partners carried out many different forms of advocacy on a national level, towards provincial governments, national ministries and societal actors, government institutions and societal actors. Whilst most partners engaged in advocacy regarding better access to services such as healthcare and education, mentioned under ‘mobilising allies’ – essential lobbying actions were undertaken in tow of our country partners, in direct response to the negative threats to the legal space. This included the fight against anti-LGBTI legislation and the involvment of UN agencies, as well as a Dutch embassy. Regional advocacy work took place at the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR), the African Union (AU) and the Treaty Monitoring Body (TMB) at the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD), which is a part of the UN. In October/November 2021, PAI conducted a human rights and international advocacy training, for the countries who were up for review at the ACHPR at the time. 31 participants from 13 different countries were equipped with practical knowledge and training on how to effectively engage the ACHPR, as well as their own states and government. During this training, PAI facilitated the development of country-specific advocacy strategies, as well as the development of a collective regional strategic on SOGIESC. These strategies include engagements before, during and after the official review. ILGA Asia supported a young transgender activist in November 2021. This activist was able to join a mission in Geneva and engage with members of the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. She held 5 meetings with the CERD committee members, the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs, International Federation for Human Rights members, and officials from the OHCHR in Geneva. Globally, there were many, many opportunities to engage in human rights and policy spaces. Due to the sheer number of these, Power of Pride prioritised the Human Rights Council (HRC), the Universal Periodic Reviews (UPRs) the UN High Level Political Forum (HLPF), the UN Commission on the Status of Women (CSW).

Finally, through support of Power of Pride, strategic plans and advocacy strategies were drafted in three of our country partners

Partners carried out many different forms of advocacy on a national level, towards provincial governments, national ministries and societal actors, government institutions and societal actors. Whilst most partners engaged in advocacy regarding better access to services such as healthcare and education, mentioned under ‘mobilising allies’ – essential lobbying actions were undertaken in tow of our country partners, in direct response to the negative threats to the legal space. This included the fight against anti-LGBTI legislation and the involvment of UN agencies, as well as a Dutch embassy. Regional advocacy work took place at the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR), the African Union (AU) and the Treaty Monitoring Body (TMB) at the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD), which is a part of the UN. In October/November 2021, PAI conducted a human rights and international advocacy training, for the countries who were up for review at the ACHPR at the time. 31 participants from 13 different countries were equipped with practical knowledge and training on how to effectively engage the ACHPR, as well as their own states and government. During this training, PAI facilitated the development of country-specific advocacy strategies, as well as the development of a collective regional strategic on SOGIESC. These strategies include engagements before, during and after the official review. ILGA Asia supported a young transgender activist in November 2021. This activist was able to join a mission in Geneva and engage with members of the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. She held 5 meetings with the CERD committee members, the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs, International Federation for Human Rights members, and officials from the OHCHR in Geneva. Globally, there were many, many opportunities to engage in human rights and policy spaces. Due to the sheer number of these, Power of Pride prioritised the Human Rights Council (HRC), the Universal Periodic Reviews (UPRs) the UN High Level Political Forum (HLPF), the UN Commission on the Status of Women (CSW).

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of policies/laws/resolutions that have been blocked in countries (through civil-society pressure) or through voting against resolutions at international forums.

title.narrative: Awareness and Acceptance raising in LGBTI individuals.

description.narrative: Individual LGBTI break out of their isolation through information sharing and sensitisation.

title.narrative: Number of actions undertaken to raise awareness and acceptance within LGBTI communities.

description.narrative: This indicatior measures actions undertaken by grassroots organisations, CBOs and CSOs to reach out to LGBTI individuals and communities for the following purposes: provision of information on SOGIESC, human rights of LGBTI people, legal rights within national and regional frameworks, building self-esteem and integrating acceptance within LGBTI individuals and communities and enabling LGBTI individuals to engage with societal structures meaningfully.

Through the programme we have worked hard to provide information to LGBTI community members, contributing to more understanding and knowledge of individual coping strategies. In one of our country partners, for instance, partners hosted a series of community round tables to discuss empowerment, SRHR, (cyber)bullying, mental health challenges, legal awareness, and socio-economic empowerment. As a result, participants of the round tables have formed their own social networks to stay in contact via group chat. In three different countries we have contributed with the programme to improving the self-esteem and knowledge on SOGIESC of 50 LGBTI living with disabilities, 20 GBMSM and transwomen living with HIV and 20 GBMSM and 83 transgender people. In another country, a partner organisation empowered and inspired young queer women creatives with a storytelling contest that led to an online campaign for youth, bringing visibility to LGBTI narratives. Finally, despite the challenges of two of our most difficult contexts, partners decided to focus on what they could do for their communities and closed 2021 with a milestone each. In one of them, partners managed to create an online space that gathers resources, promotes awareness, and mitigates the isolation of individuals who lack a physical community. In the other one, partners decided to make psychosocial counselling available for 60 LBQT community members.

title.narrative: Number of capacity building initiatives undertaken

description.narrative: Capacity building inniciatives includes: L&A skills trainings (first and second tier) provided on international and regional mechanisms, workshops, panels and side-events organised/participated, L&A engagement coaching sessions provided to LGBTI activists for international and regional mechanisms and the technical advocacy support that was provided to CSOs, CBOs or activists by the PoP Alliance.
